interactions: Dexamethasone + phenytoin or fosphenytoin: phenytoin induces CYP3A4 and lowers dexamethasone exposure, and dexamethasone can change phenytoin levels; risk of losing edema control; avoid, or raise the steroid dose and monitor phenytoin levels.
Dexamethasone + carbamazepine or phenobarbital: CYP3A4 induction lowers dexamethasone exposure; avoid.
Levetiracetam + dexamethasone, temozolomide, ondansetron or omeprazole: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally eliminated without CYP metabolism.
Valproate + temozolomide: additive thrombocytopenia; valproate modestly reduces temozolomide clearance; monitor platelets.
Phenytoin or carbamazepine + temozolomide: no clinically relevant effect on temozolomide exposure (non-enzymatic activation).
Lacosamide + ondansetron: lacosamide prolongs PR and ondansetron prolongs QT; obtain an ECG before IV loading.
Omeprazole + phenytoin: CYP2C19 inhibition can raise phenytoin levels; monitor levels if phenytoin is used.
Dexamethasone + metformin: steroid-induced hyperglycemia; monitor glucose and add insulin as needed.
output.proposed: Lorazepam and a second-line antiseizure medication (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate or lacosamide) with dexamethasone, temozolomide, ondansetron, metformin, lisinopril and omeprazole
warnings: Lorazepam: additive respiratory depression with other sedatives; monitor airway in a patient with reduced consciousness.

output.query: Status epilepticus treatment and seizures in glioblastoma

results.finding: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus.
Continuous EEG is recommended when non-convulsive status epilepticus is suspected or consciousness does not recover.
In glioma, antiseizure medication is given after a first seizure, enzyme-inducing drugs are avoided, and corticosteroids are used for symptomatic edema at the lowest effective dose.

output.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine [Glauser_2016], and levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019]. Continuous EEG is needed to detect non-convulsive seizures when consciousness does not recover [Brophy_2012]. In glioma, enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs are avoided and corticosteroids treat symptomatic edema [EANO_2021].

action_criteria.rationale: Status epilepticus in a treated glioblastoma needs MRI to show progression and edema, which decide the steroid dose and oncological management [Brophy_2012; EANO_2021].

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT perform LP without MRI assessment of mass effect first
Do NOT choose an enzyme-inducing ASM (phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine): induction lowers dexamethasone exposure while edema control depends on it
Do NOT defer steroid re-escalation while waiting for full imaging confirmation if MRI shows worsening edema
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg) on top of his maintenance dose, and avoid fosphenytoin because CYP3A4 induction lowers dexamethasone exposure while edema control depends on it [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Re-escalate dexamethasone for symptomatic peritumoral edema, at least back to the pre-taper 12 mg per day, with capillary glucose monitoring and insulin as needed given his diabetes [EANO_2021].
Refer to neuro-oncology and neurosurgery for the tumor progression (re-resection, re-irradiation or systemic options) [EANO_2021].

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac question; recurrent GBM with edema explains presentation.
No arrhythmogenic concern beyond standard ICU monitoring.
Amyloid PET / DaTscan irrelevant to SE in known GBM.
LP is relatively contraindicated with a known intracranial mass and increased peritumoral edema (herniation risk), and nothing in the case suggests CNS infection.

The seizure focus is the progressing tumor on MRI; no feature calls for antibody testing
Temozolomide and dexamethasone do not commonly cause SE; the MRI shows a structural driver

key_clinical_evidence: Patients with brain tumors entering SE require simultaneous tumor-edema control (steroids) and ASM escalation; neither alone is sufficient
Dexamethasone tapers in glioma patients commonly precipitate breakthrough seizures via increased peritumoral edema
Levetiracetam is preferred in glioma because enzyme-inducing ASMs lower corticosteroid exposure and interact with many systemic agents [EANO_2021]
An ASM level within the reference range does not exclude breakthrough seizures
LP in a patient with known intracranial mass and edema risks herniation; MRI must guide the decision

patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old White male retired electrician was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his wife called 911. She reported witnessing a brief generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds while he was sitting at the breakfast table. She noted he had been 'not himself' for the past three weeks — increasingly forgetful, more apathetic, and seeming confused in the mornings. After the witnessed seizure stopped, she expected him to recover within minutes as had occurred with prior episodes, but he remained minimally responsive and confused for over 25 minutes, prompting her call to 911. He has a known diagnosis of right temporal glioblastoma (GBM) diagnosed 8 months ago, status post gross total resection followed by concurrent temozolomide and radiation, now on maintenance temozolomide. He completed his most recent temozolomide cycle 11 days ago. He takes dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for peritumoral edema, which was recently tapered from 6 mg twice daily over the past two weeks per his neuro-oncologist's instruction. He has a known seizure disorder secondary to his brain tumor and takes levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. His wife reports he has been taking his levetiracetam consistently. His wife reports no fever or headache in recent days.
